articles.title: Geoffrey Omedo: Unpacking the myths, good, bad, ugly of carbon markets in Africa - EnviroNews Nigeria
articles.summary: Geoffrey Omedo: Unpacking the myths, good, bad, ugly of carbon markets in Africa  EnviroNews Nigeria
articles.full_text:
As the Carbon Markets Summit begins in Kigali, Rwanda, this week, with the participation of the African Union, AUDA-NEPAD, the European Commission, UNDP, the UNFCCC, the African Development Bank, DBSA, among many other partners, I share my 18-year perspective and reflections on this vital subject in this week’s 20th Edition of the #Africa #Energy #Finance #Pulse.
The year was 2008.
The air in our Nairobi office, ensconced in the lush greenery neighbouring Karura Forest within the United Nations Office in Nairobi, was palpable with anticipation. During our unit meetings, detailed progress on a flagship carbon market project for the Clean Development Mechanism that Kenya was advancing would be discussed.
Unfortunately, the project struggled to go beyond the Project Design Document stage!
This was the Mumias Sugar 35 MW Bagasse Cogeneration Project in Western Kenya (later formally registered as UNFCCC CDM Project Ref. 1404 on 04 December 2008). Designed to harness sugarcane milling residue – where Mumias Sugar Company (now sadly under receivership) crushed roughly 2.4 million tonnes of cane annually, generating an enormous 37% bagasse yield (an estimated 890,000 tonnes).
This initiative was designed to replace inefficient low-pressure boilers with modern high-pressure steam boilers and turbo-alternators. The technical design allowed the plant to use around 9 MW internally while exporting 26 MW of clean, renewable electricity to the Kenya Power and Lighting Company (KPLC) national grid, generating projected baseline reductions between 129,591 and 157,982 tonnes of metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year by displacing grid thermal power and avoiding open-air bagasse decomposition and methane off-gassing.
Sounds easy, right?
Just from this initiative, I learned that carbon market projects were not a walk in the park – as policy constraints (monopolistic tendencies in generation) basically made the project untenable.
The Kenya Tea Development Agency Carbon Project Example
This was the second carbon project that we worked on in 2011-2012.
This was an innovative fuelwood decommissioning project for the Kenya Tea Development Agency (KTDA). What many people do not realise is that, for drying (curing) the black tea we enjoy taking for breakfast, immense volumes of wood fuel are consumed in factory boilers.
The result?
Massive pollution, deforestation, and degradation.
If you have ever traveled up toward Kenya’s Kericho Highlands or the slopes of Mount Kenya where tea is grown, you have seen those expansive, scenic plush lands covered by green, undulating waves of tea bushes disappearing into the mist-covered horizon.
This carbon project wanted to preserve those indigenous water towers by switching factory boilers away from forest timber.
Sounds easy, again, right? But not too fast…
As the team worked to painstakingly get these project concept note design documents – collecting the much-needed data required through the rigorous validation machinery of the UNFCCC’s Clean Development Mechanism (CDM)- something drastic happened.
The global carbon markets crashed….
This happened after the European Union restricted international Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) in Phase 3 of the EU ETS post-2012, thereby leading to secondary credit prices plummeting from over €20 per tonne to below €0.50.
This was devastating – especially to project developers on the African continent.
In Kenya, only a small number of large utility initiatives – most notably the Olkaria II Geothermal Expansion Project (UNFCCC CDM Project Ref. 3773, registered on 16 December 2010) and Olkaria III – managed to achieve commercial CER issuance before the market collapsed.
Across the entire Kyoto commitment period, the African continent secured less than 15% of registered CDM activities, with Sub-Saharan Africa capturing under 3% of standalone projects. The overwhelming beneficiary of the CDM was Asia, which absorbed over 70% of global issuances by destroying industrial gases in large chemical facilities, leaving Africa’s decentralised, high-co-benefit agro-industrial projects stranded.
From Kyoto’s CDM – to Paris Agreement’s Carbon Market Regimes
Today, under the Paris Agreement, the carbon pendulum is swinging back.
With the operationalisation of the new compliance regime (Article 6 of the Paris Agreement), there are rising compliance obligations from some premium buyers – especially international aviation under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). We also now have an institutional shift toward durable nature-based and engineered removals. Blue bond carbon markets are also emerging – where the continent equally stands at a pole position.
In fact, I daresay that Africa is now no longer on the periphery of the carbon markets.
Yet, as these markets open up opportunities on the continent, it is important to cut through conference declarations and examine the sector with rigorous, clear-eyed reality.
Here is my take on The Myths, The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly of Carbon Markets.
The Good
Africa is Rich in Carbon Stocks….Super Rich!
The “Good” begins with Africa’s huge untapped natural carbon balance. The continent is a vital ecological anchor for planetary climate stabilisation.
Let me just emphasise the Congo Basin -as an example.
At the heart of Central Africa lies the Congo River Basin, spanning 3.7 million square kilometres. Estimated to be sequestering a net 1.5 billion tonnes of atmospheric carbon annually, it remains one of the world’s few intact net tropical carbon sinks. For example, located within this basin is the Cuvette Centrale peatland complex, shared between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Congo. Covering 16.7 million hectares (ranging between 145,500 and 167,000 square kilometres), this subterranean formation locks away a median below-ground carbon stock of 30.6 petagrams of carbon – roughly 30 billion metric tonnes of carbon.
Add to this the AfriMont consortium’s findings across 44 forest monitoring plots in 12 African nations-which established that African tropical montane forests store an average of 150 megagrams of carbon per hectare in aboveground biomass (exceeding unit-area biomass in the Amazon Basin) – along with coastal mangrove belts storing 218 tonnes per hectare across deep sedimentary substrates, and Africa’s ecological significance is clear.
Even more…..but the methodology to account for avoided emissions/removals in this sector still remains riddled with significant uncertainties!
Regulation – The Move to Sovereign Governance
What makes this cycle fundamentally different from our 2008 experience is that African governments are no longer passive project hosts.
Unlike during the CDM era, Africa is hard at work building the systems and structures needed to galvanise a robust carbon market edifice. As illustrated above, we are now transitioning from speculative policy toward robust, operational registry architectures to mobilise climate finance.
A few examples suffice here below:
Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa lead with fully operational carbon registries, such as Kenya’s National Carbon Registry (KNCR) and Ghana’s EPA Carbon Market Office, which has already executed the continent’s first end-to-end Article 6.2 transfer of 11,733 ITMOs to Switzerland.
They are followed by nations like Rwanda, Zambia, Malawi, Tanzania, Senegal, and Gabon, which are actively validating projects and securing bilateral frameworks, such as Zambia’s 1.6 million authorised ITMOs with Switzerland.
Meanwhile, countries like Nigeria – which has even launched the Lagos State’s sub-national registry – and Zimbabwe, with its sovereign royalty framework, are carving out new regulatory frontiers.
With 35 bilateral agreements, 12 host countries with active tracks, and 91 approved PACM activities, Africa’s structured governance models and digital MRV pipelines are proving that the continent is actively organising to turn its vast renewable and natural assets into sovereign, sustainable wealth. Out of these, an estimated 2.73 million ITMOs have formally been transferred or received.
Yet, a lot of work is still needed!
Despite the political momentum surrounding Article 6 and voluntary market monetization, national readiness remains dismally low – as out of 55 African Union member states, only nine have managed to stand up dedicated registry infrastructure: Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, Zambia, Tanzania, Rwanda, Gabon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Nigeria.
While another 16 nations report being in varying stages of pipeline development, the reality is that roughly 84% of the continent still lacks the sovereign digital architecture required to verify emission baselines, prevent double counting, issue statutory Letters of Authorisation, and execute corresponding adjustments.
Without these registries, the vast majority of African nations remain exposed to carbon leakage and unable to convert their massive natural and technological abatement potential into credible, high-integrity sovereign assets.
Across the continent, the following are major Article 6 carbon policy signals to watch for:
- Kenya – Holding five bilateral agreements, the government has recently codified a controversial statutory 10 million tonne transfer cap through 2030 to ostensibly protect its own Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) balance sheet. It has also mandated that land-based projects return at least 40% of aggregate annual earnings to local communities through registered Community Development Agreements.
  - Ghana – Leading transaction-oriented governance, it executed the continent’s first end-to-end Article 6.2 transfer of 11,733 ITMOs to Switzerland generated by Envirofit clean cookstoves. It is managing an operational registry integrated with the UNFCCC Centralized Accounting and Reporting Platform, charging an explicit $3 to $5 per tonne administrative ITMO fee.
  - Senegal – Accounts for eight approved PACM activiti

articles.title: J&K bets on waste-to-wealth model, sets 10-year circular economy roadmap - Greater Kashmir
articles.summary: J&K bets on waste-to-wealth model, sets 10-year circular economy roadmap  Greater Kashmir
articles.full_text:
Srinagar, Oct 12: The government has notified the Circular Economy Policy 2026, setting out a 10-year roadmap to reduce waste generation, promote recycling and resource recovery, and create employment opportunities through sustainable enterprises across Jammu and Kashmir.
The policy, notified by the Housing and Urban Development Department through Government Order No 208-JK(HUD) of 2026, envisages a shift from conventional waste disposal towards a system in which materials are recovered, reused, recycled, and channelled back into productive economic activities. 
The policy identifies a baseline financial scenario of Rs 3548.7 crore over 10 years to guide planning and expenditure assessment. However, the amount does not constitute an automatic budgetary allocation, with individual projects required to undergo eligibility assessment, technical appraisal, administrative approval and financial concurrence before implementation.
The Housing and Urban Development Department has been designated as the nodal department for implementing the policy, which has been developed with inputs from the Centre for Innovation and Transformation in Governance (CITaG) and the Planning, Development and Monitoring Department.
The framework seeks to integrate waste management with economic development, particularly in sectors such as horticulture, tourism, construction, food processing, traditional crafts and municipal services.  
It also envisages greater participation by self-help groups, micro, small and medium enterprises, startups and informal waste workers in the emerging circular economy.
A key feature of the policy is the introduction of a three-tier framework for urban local bodies, recognising differences in population, waste generation, geography, infrastructure and institutional capacity across J&K.
Under the proposed arrangement, smaller and remote urban local bodies will focus on source segregation, recycling, reuse, repair and decentralised waste processing. Medium-sized and corridor-linked towns will be encouraged to develop aggregation facilities, community composting and small biogas plants where feasible.
Meanwhile, Srinagar and Jammu have been identified for a more integrated circular-economy model involving city-wide waste segregation, construction and demolition waste processing, compressed biogas and biomethanation, and treated-wastewater reuse from sewage treatment plants.
The policy states that urban local bodies will be categorised according to waste generation, geographical location, availability of segregated waste, processing infrastructure, and financial readiness. 
The categorisation will be reviewed periodically, allowing local bodies to move to a higher category as their institutional and operational capacities improve.
The government has identified municipal solid waste, organic waste, plastic and packaging materials, horticulture biomass, orchard residues, food-processing waste, construction debris, wastewater, electronic waste, and discarded products as priority areas for intervention.
In the horticulture sector, the policy envisages developing systems to collect and process orchard residues, rejected produce, vegetable-market waste and food-processing by-products. 
These materials could be converted into compost, bio-inputs and other marketable products, creating additional economic value while reducing the volume of waste sent for disposal.
The policy also seeks to address post-harvest losses through improved aggregation, storage, transportation and processing facilities. 
The proposed approach is intended to connect waste recovery with the needs of horticulture-based enterprises and local markets.
Tourism and pilgrimage have been identified as another important area, given the seasonal concentration of visitors and the resulting pressure on municipal infrastructure. 
Hotels, restaurants, religious institutions, event venues, and pilgrimage-related establishments will be required to follow applicable waste segregation and management requirements.
The policy envisages destination-specific waste collection arrangements, improved food-waste management, and stronger compliance monitoring to address the environmental pressures associated with tourism and pilgrimage activities.
Construction and demolition waste will be handled through designated collection points, transportation tracking, and authorised processing facilities. 
Recovered materials, including recycled aggregates, could be used in public works and other suitable applications, subject to technical standards and applicable approvals.
The policy also seeks to promote repair, refurbishment and reuse markets for furniture, appliances, textiles, handicrafts, and other products. 
By extending the useful life of discarded goods, the government aims to reduce waste while creating opportunities for small businesses and skilled workers.
Mandatory segregation at source is among the principal regulatory measures proposed under the framework. 
Households, commercial establishments, institutions, and other waste generators will be expected to separate waste and channel it through approved collection and processing systems.
Bulk waste generators, including hotels, hospitals, markets, commercial complexes, transport terminals, and large institutions will face specific compliance requirements covering registration, waste minimisation, segregation and reporting. 
Depending on feasibility and applicable rules, these establishments may also be required to undertake on-site processing or use authorised treatment facilities.
The policy proposes inspections, compliance notices, corrective measures and graded enforcement against violations. 
It also envisages incentives for entities demonstrating sustained compliance, including public recognition and procurement preferences where permissible.
To support implementation, the government has proposed six priority circular-economy clusters covering Jammu's urban materials recovery and construction waste, organic waste and packaging in the Valley, horticulture biomass and packaging, pilgrimage and tourism services, artisan and repair-based enterprises, and decentralised livelihoods in mountainous areas. 
A further cluster has been proposed for urban water reuse and sludge-linked circularity.
The cluster-based model is intended to connect waste generation with collection, processing, transportation, markets and enterprise development. 
The policy argues that geographically linked systems could reduce transportation costs, improve the availability of recoverable materials and make waste-processing investments more viable.
Employment generation is another major component of the policy. 
It envisages integrating informal waste pickers and sanitation workers into formal value chains through registration, training, occupational safety measures and access to structured employment opportunities.
The document sets a baseline fifth-year target of integrating 60 percent of informal waste and sanitation workers into formal value chains, supporting 50 circular-economy startups, training or apprenticing 10,000 youth in circular occupations, and integrating 2,500 artisan, repair and refurbishment enterprises into circular markets.
It also sets a baseline target of linking 5,000 street vendors or micro-retailers to low-waste services and creating or formalising 15,000 green jobs and livelihoods. 
These figures are policy targets under the baseline scenario and do not represent jobs or enterprises already created.
The government proposes to support eligible activities through convergence with existing schemes and programmes, including Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0, AMRUT 2.0 and relevant livelihood, skill-development and enterprise-support initiatives.
The financing framework also envisages municipal resources, user charges, private investment, public-private partnerships and extended producer responsibility-linked mechanisms. 
However, the policy makes clear that funding will depend on project eligibility, appraisal, approvals and the availability of resources under the relevant schemes and budgetary provisions.
The order specifically states that no GST reimbursement, GST reduction or tax waiver is being approved under the policy.
A digital monitoring system is also proposed to track waste generation, segregation, collection, transportation, processing and disposal. 
The planned digital ledger and urban local body dashboards are intended to improve record-keeping, compliance monitoring and accountability, while geographic information systems will support infrastructure planning and the tracking of waste flows.
The proposed institutional structure includes a J&K Circular Economy Mission, a Circular Economy Cell, district-level coordination mechanisms and implementation arrangements within urban local bodies. 
The Housing and Urban Development Department will coordinate with departments dealing with agriculture, horticulture, tourism, industries, commerce, environment, rural development, and skill development.
The policy will remain in force for 10 years, with provision for review every three years or earlier, depending on changes in national regulations, implementation experience, financing conditions, and government directions.
The government has authorised the Housing and Urban Development Department to issue operational guidelines, model bylaws, standard operating procedures, and monitoring formats for implementation.

Circular Economy Event's 29th Edition Programme Highlights E-Waste, Batteries and Critical Raw Materials
The 29th edition of an international circular economy event, organised by Italian Exhibition Group, has had its programme developed by the Ecomondos International Technical Scientific Committee together with public and private partners, according to Recycling International.
Recycling of waste electrical and electronic equipment and waste batteries sits among the programme's central themes, with a dedicated event titled Circular Economy in Action: e-waste and waste batteries best practices set to review European experience in recovering critical raw materials.
That session is expected to analyse the Italian situation and consider how recycling of such equipment and batteries can lessen Europe's reliance on imported materials.
A further discussion, EU-Africa Strategic Corridors to a mutually beneficial cooperation for critical raw materials, will also take up the critical raw materials question.
Plastic recycling is scheduled for treatment in Plastic circularity: new perspectives and critical issues, which will look at European measures intended to support resource efficiency and the shift to a circular economy.
Additional talks will consider the Circular Economy Act and what it means for packaging and waste management in Europe.
Textiles form another major strand, with sessions on reuse, repair, ecodesign and extended producer responsibility, while traceability and transparency across the value chain are also on the agenda alongside the European Sustainable Products Regulation and digital product passports.
The built environment will be addressed through urban mining, regulatory frameworks and technologies that support circular models in construction, with a separate event intended to prompt dialogue on speeding up circularity in construction and infrastructure.
A workshop will additionally look at how circularity can be measured along the value chain.
Paper recycling will appear at the Paper District GDO & Grocery Summit, where sustainability, regulatory compliance and market trends in the relationship between the paper industry and large-scale retail will be examined.
Comieco, working with Nomisma, will present an assessment of the environmental and economic benefits of National Recovery and Resilience Plan-funded projects connected to paper recycling.
The programme also extends to biodegradable and compostable bioplastics, soil protection, agricultural innovation and the circular bioeconomy, with the 28th National Conference on composting and anaerobic digestion held alongside the fifth States General for Soil Health conference.
Water resources and the blue economy feature in sessions on coastal regeneration, urban water services, pollution prevention, water efficiency and smart infrastructure.
International discussions will cover resource recovery from end-of-life products and materials in the Mediterranean, oil pollution, sustainable materials and water resilience.
The sixth Africa Green Growth Forum will centre on the Mattei Plan and sustainable development in Africa, with particular attention to water and agriculture.
Financing sessions will examine climate transition plans and environmental, social and governance risk management, together with investment models for innovation and competitiveness.
Regulatory discussions are set to cover waste management, traceability, compliance, landfill standards and end-of-waste criteria.
Among the key events are the fifth Forum on Responsible Communication and the third ESG CEO Summit.
The programme will also include calls for papers on waste prevention, circular resource management and industrial symbiosis, along with discussions on scaling cleantech innovation.

articles.summary: Ecomondo 2026 to showcase recycling and the circular economy  Recycling International
articles.full_text:
More than 70 events, conferences and workshops covering recycling, resource efficiency and the challenges shaping the global ecological transition will be presented at Ecomondo 2026 at Rimini Expo Centre from 3-6 November
The programme for the 29th edition of the international event, organised by Italian Exhibition Group (IEG), has been developed by Ecomondo’s International Technical Scientific Committee in collaboration with public and private partners.
Critical raw materials
The recycling of waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) and waste batteries will be among the programme’s key topics.An event, ‘Circular Economy in Action: e-waste and waste batteries best practices’, will examine European experiences in recycling critical raw materials. It will analyse the situation in Italy and assess how WEEE and battery recycling can reduce Europe’s dependence on imports.
Critical raw materials will also be addressed through ‘EU-Africa Strategic Corridors to a mutually beneficial cooperation for critical raw materials’.
Meanwhile, plastic recycling will feature in ‘Plastic circularity: new perspectives and critical issues’, focusing on European measures to support resource efficiency and the transition towards a circular economy. Other discussions will examine the Circular Economy Act and its implications for European packaging and waste management.
Textiles and construction
Textiles will be another major focus, with sessions addressing reuse, repair, ecodesign and extended producer responsibility. With an emphasis on traceability and transparency throughout the value chain, the programme will also consider the European Sustainable Products Regulation and digital product passports,
The built environment will be covered through discussions on urban mining, regulatory frameworks and technologies supporting circular economy models in construction. A separate eventwill encourage dialogue on accelerating circularity in construction and infrastructure. Another workshop will examine how circularity can be measured across the value chain.
Paper, bioeconomy and composting
Paper recycling will feature at the Paper District GDO & Grocery Summit. The event will examine sustainability, regulatory compliance and market trends in relations between the paper industry and large-scale retail.
Comieco, working with Nomisma, will present an assessment of the environmental and economic benefits of National Recovery and Resilience Plan-funded projects relating to paper recycling.
The programme will also cover biodegradable and compostable bioplastics, soil protection, agricultural innovation and the circular bioeconomy. The 28th National Conference on composting and anaerobic digestion will take place alongside the fifth States General for Soil Health conference.
Water and international cooperation
Water resources and the blue economy will feature sessions on coastal regeneration, urban water services, pollution prevention, water efficiency and smart infrastructure.International discussions will address resource recovery from end-of-life products and materials in the Mediterranean, oil pollution, sustainable materials and water resilience.
The sixth Africa Green Growth Forum will focus on the Mattei Plan and sustainable development in Africa, particularly water and agriculture.
Financing and regulation
Financing sessions will examine climate transition plans and environmental, social and governance risk management, alongside investment models for innovation and competitiveness.Regulatory discussions will cover waste management, traceability, compliance, landfill standards and end-of-waste criteria.
Key events include the fifth Forum on Responsible Communication and the third ESG CEO Summit.
The programme will also include calls for papers on waste prevention, circular resource management and industrial symbiosis, alongside discussions on scaling cleantech innovation.
The full programme is available at: https://www.ecomondo.com/en/events/conferences/program

Its Home Galaxy Surprised Astronomers.  ScienceAlertWebb Measures Distance to Farthest Fast Radio Burst, Suggesting Origin  NASA Science (.gov)Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away  The GuardianJames Webb telescope pinpoints the most distant 'fast radio burst' ever seen, more than 10 billion light-years away  Live ScienceFast Radio Burst ...
articles.full_text:
Sometimes we receive strange, ghostly radio signals from outer space, which astronomers have yet to conclusively explain.
Partially because they disappear almost as soon as they arrive.
The ephemera known as fast radio bursts (FRBs) are among the Universe's most mysterious occurrences, even more eerie than the supposed little green aliens with a penchant for physical probes.
If they were related, that would neatly solve two major mysteries.
But FRBs are bursts of radio waves from the distant cosmos, generally lasting for tiny fractions of a second (i.e., fast).
Their transience, and the fact that they randomly appear across the sky, have made it difficult to pin down their origins for nearly two decades since their discovery in 2007.
But we just got a huge clue: Astronomers have reported the most distant FRB yet, designated FRB 20240304B, a burst of ancient energy that was emitted in one-thousandth of a second and has traveled through 80 percent of the Universe's history to meet us.
"What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them," explains lead author Manisha Caleb, a radio astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of Sydney.
"We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof."
So, who's the cosmic culprit in this specific case? Possibly a magnetar: a type of neutron star on steroids that packs the most powerful magnetic fields in the Universe and squeezes the mass of a whole Sun into a magnetic marble the size of San Francisco Bay.
Yet here's another conundrum: despite their incomprehensibly intense origins, and their ability to release 500 million Suns' worth of energy in thousandths of a second, they may be light(er)weights compared to other stellar outbursts, which has led to a sampler platter of possibilities and added to the difficulty of their conclusive identification:
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time." – astronomer and astrophysicist J. Xavier Prochaska
"Fundamentally, it is because the energies involved are modest. They are extreme for radio wave emission, but nothing like the energy in a supernova or gamma-ray burst," J. Xavier Prochaska, an astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told ScienceAlert.
"As such, theorists have devised nearly 100 models to generate them.
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time."
In the study, published in the journal Science, a massive, international collaboration of astronomers used multiple observatories to explore this mysterious FRB emanating from 'cosmic noon,' an era only 3 billion years after the Big Bang when Universal star formation was at its peak.
The astronomers identified the FRB in March 2024 using MeerKAT, a 64-antenna radio telescope in South Africa's Meerkat National Park.
They then pointed two ultra-sensitive ground telescopes at the corresponding patch of sky to see its host galaxy and discovered… darkness.
They looked as deep as they could "but there was simply nothing to see," Prochaska says.
So they called in the heavy orbital artillery (just a metaphor, for now), the JWST and its exceptional infrared sensitivity.
And if the researchers suspected a monster, they found a mouse:
"We thought it would be a big, nicely formed galaxy with lots of stars, and instead it was a little dwarf galaxy, although it was actively forming stars," says Caleb.
Altogether, this dwarf galaxy is 1,000 times less massive than expected.
It's also exceedingly young, with 90 percent of its stellar mass having formed in the past 30 million years.
This helped the astronomers favor a magnetar as the potential source of the historic FRB.
Another prominent FRB scenario involves the collision of two neutron stars, a cataclysmic crash that yields a black hole or an extra-heavy neutron star, plus a bunch of literal gold.
Yet neutron stars dance around each other for billions of years before colliding, like a still-shy couple on a second date, so it wouldn't make sense in a young galaxy.
Magnetars, however, can form and release their magnetic energy in just millions of years. Especially in a metal-poor galaxy like this that breeds massive stars.
Also, like good guests, FRBs come bearing gifts of the astrophysical kind.
Even though light travels at the speed of itself, the ultimate breakneck physical limit, it only does so in a vacuum.
And as this FRB passed through the cold, ionized (electrically charged) gas that permeates the cosmos, its lower-frequency waves were slowed more than its higher ones, so they arrived later.
Turbulent gas, most likely in its home galaxy, also scattered the signal, smearing it out over several milliseconds
FRBs thus act as an astronomical flashlight, and this particular one has had its signal warped by two cosmic-scale structures as it traversed most of the Universe to meet us.
In doing so, it helped illuminate an unknown galaxy group along the way, located about 3.5 billion light-years away, while also bearing the ionic imprint of the Virgo Cluster, the nearest such structure to Earth, only around 54 million light-years distant.
Finally, since we only know of about 100 FRBs whose host galaxies have been confirmed, the researchers note, and most are billions of light-years more local, this wasn't just the cherry atop the celestial sundae, but a whole other sundae on top of the sundae.
"Because we have scant understanding of what generates FRBs, we could only hope that they might exist at such early times," Prochaska told ScienceAlert.
"Now, we have proven it and this will drive new, dedicated studies to find others – and search even greater distances!"
The research has been published in Science.

articles.title: An abandoned rock sample could prove life once existed on Mars. But will it ever reach Earth? - CNN
articles.summary: An abandoned rock sample could prove life once existed on Mars. But will it ever reach Earth?  CNN
articles.full_text:
A leopard-spotted rock that could prove whether life ever existed beyond Earth is sitting in a tube on Mars.
NASA’s Perseverance rover grabbed up the sample, called Sapphire Canyon, from rocky outcrops on the edges of the Neretva Vallis, a valley sculpted by rivers that once flowed into an ancient lake in Jezero Crater more than 3 billion years ago. The rover landed at the dried lakebed in February 2021 for expressly this purpose, hunting for rocks created or modified by water in the past, which would have had the best chance of preserving evidence of life.
Members of the Perseverance science team have said the Sapphire Canyon sample, about the size of a chalk stick, is exactly the type of rock they hoped the rover would discover.
“This is the first time I think we’ve found something that qualifies as a ‘potential biosignature’” on Mars, said Adrian Broz, a member of Perseverance’s science team and a postdoctoral researcher in the Planetary Surface Processes Lab at Purdue University in Indiana. “It’s currently sealed inside of Perseverance rover’s chassis, and it sits there quietly and awaits return to Earth.”
But the sample might not make it to our planet, at least not anytime soon.
The Mars Sample Return program, a joint venture by NASA and the European Space Agency to ferry the promising cache back to Earth, attracted intense scrutiny for its high price tag and complex design. After sinking billions of dollars into the endeavor, NASA paused and began reassessing the program in 2024 before canceling it entirely — with no clear alternative in sight.
“While Perseverance’s samples remain safely stored on Mars, NASA is exploring a range of potential return options that could offer simpler and more affordable approaches than the original Mars Sample Return plan, including possible commercial or international contributions,” the agency said in a statement shared with CNN in July. NASA’s leaders still haven’t revealed a path forward.
And while the discovery of the Sapphire Canyon sample is building a strong case for the existence of ancient microbial life on Mars, there’s only so much scientists can learn from afar, said Dr. Briony Horgan, professor of Earth, atmospheric and planetary sciences at Purdue University.
The rover, which cost NASA about $2.4 billion to build and launch, doesn’t have the instrument suite to answer such lofty questions by itself on the red planet.
“We can keep doing these studies and coming up with these hints, but we’re never going to know for sure until we get those samples back,” said Horgan, also a coinvestigator and planner on the Perseverance team. “These samples are our best current chance for really understanding is life abundant and common, or is Earth truly unique?”
Now, it’s possible one of NASA’s biggest competitors in the new space race will be the first to achieve Mars sample retrieval: China is looking to pick up its own souvenir from the red planet in 2031, and it has taken steps to ensure success by designing a mission that’s similar to one it pulled off two years ago. But the rocks returned by the country’s Tianwen-3 mission, expected to launch in 2028, could look very different — and perhaps offer different insights — from Perseverance’s samples, depending on how plans evolve.
‘Scientific holy grail’
Scientists consider Sapphire Canyon such a promising find because of its spotted appearance. On Earth, the tiny dots, called reaction fronts or reduction spots, form in soils and sediments due to the presence of microbial activity.
“When there’s organic matter that’s lodged in sediment or soil that’s buried and microbes start to digest some of that organic matter, they form these bleached halos and spots that are quite resemblant to the ones that Perseverance found in this ancient river valley,” said Broz, coauthor of a study about the rock sample published in September 2025.
Perseverance drilled the Sapphire Canyon sample from an arrowhead-shaped rock called Cheyava Falls in July 2024. The mudstones surrounding the rock were also covered in hundreds of thousands of promising reduction spots potentially made by ancient microscopic life.
Still, returning the samples to Earth is the only way to determine whether these distinctive features were formed by the presence of life, or abiotically — through chemical or geological processes that did not require life, Broz said.
It’s a lesson planetary scientists learned from studying the famed Allan Hills 84001 Martian meteorite, uncovered in the Antarctic in 1984 and originally thought to contain the remnants of ancient life. Multiple groups of scientists analyzed samples from the meteorite, discovering that nonbiological, geological processes left behind signatures that could be misinterpreted as organic carbon compounds attributed to life.
“Even when you have all the labs all over the world looking at a rock that has putative evidence of ancient life, it is a really difficult thing to do, and so you want to just be able to apply every technique you can think of in all the best labs,” said Ashwin Vasavada, project scientist for the Curiosity rover at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California.
The rover’s onboard tools can offer some data, but they weren’t designed to do the kind of analysis necessary to make definitive answers because that wasn’t part of the original plan.
“The science instruments had been selected with the assumption that they would be doing reconnaissance for sample selection and providing the geologic context on Mars for samples that were always expected to be returned to Earth,” said Dr. Melissa Rice, a professor of planetary science at Western Washington University who has worked on NASA rover missions for over two decades.
The first entry in NASA’s budget request to Congress for initial studies of a Mars sample return program occurred in the fiscal year 1978, according to Casey Dreier, chief of space policy at The Planetary Society. The request was made on the heels of the agency’s Viking missions to Mars, considered NASA’s first attempt to search for evidence of life on the red planet.
“It tells you how long it has remained this kind of scientific holy grail for Mars,” Dreier said.
A 2003 survey identifying top scientific objectives for future space missions — and several subsequent reports — highlighted retrieving red planet samples as a key priority, which led to Mars Sample Return becoming intertwined with the Perseverance rover’s mission. The two projects were developed hand in hand.
A complicated path
The original concept for Mars Sample Return, shared in 2020, included a succession of multiple missions launching from Earth to Mars: a lander containing a Mars fetch rover to collect the samples and an ascent vehicle to return the samples to Earth by 2031 at the earliest.
The ascent vehicle was intended to shoot out a football-size container holding the samples that would be captured by a separately launched ESA spacecraft orbiting Mars.
Then, the ESA orbiter would head back to Earth, transferring the sample container into yet another vehicle that could deploy from the orbiter and safely land the samples on our planet.
By 2022, the plan shifted: Perseverance would deliver the sample suite to the Mars Ascent Vehicle that would launch on a return journey. The lander would carry two small recovery helicopters, which could grab samples from the rover if Perseverance wasn’t in good enough condition to make the drive to a landing site. This nudged the return date to 2033.
As things progressed, assessments from independent review boards pointed out how unwieldy and complex the retrieval process had become. The program’s budget ballooned to an eye-popping maximum of $11 billion and the estimated return date for the samples pushed to 2040. NASA also faced budget cuts for the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years, and the excessive costs of the mission led to waning political support for the program.
The agency put out a call for cheaper, quicker and less complex proposals and, in January 2025, identified two strategies that relied on commercial partnerships or leaned on previously used Mars landing technology so as to not reinvent the wheel. That assessment came out just weeks before President Donald Trump took office and began the search for a new NASA administrator.
The next sample return update, revealed with NASA’s fiscal year 2026 budget request, was an abrupt blow: “NASA plans to terminate the Mars Sample Return Program given that current architecture options remain unaffordable. It is anticipated that future missions to Mars will return samples for study on Earth.”
The agency’s 2027 budget request didn’t mention the program at all. NASA spent about $2.5 billion on the Mars Sample Return through its cancellation, Dreier said.
However, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman has mentioned that he’s interested in getting Perseverance’s samples delivered to Earth.
“As I’ve said many times, I think retrieving the samples from Mars can lead to the most significant scientific breakthrough in human history,” Isaacman said at a news conference on August 30 after the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. “There’s no question we’re going to go get samples, whether it’s robotic or whether it’s astronauts picking it up will be the question, and certainly the time frame associated with it.”
Speaking at the All-In Summit in September, Isaacman blamed his predecessors for the program’s failures, noting “the prior administration canceled the Mars Sample Return mission that was on track to cost more than an aircraft carrier.”
While the finger-pointing about the fate of the original program appears to continue, no additional details about next steps have emerged.

BNP Paribas Asset Management (BNPP AM) has launched its Global Sustainability Strategy 2026–2030, setting out a six-pillar roadmap to strengthen investment resilience and long-term value creation. The strategy covers more […]

articles.full_text:
BNP Paribas Asset Management Launches 2030 Sustainability Strategy
- $1.97 trillion in assets: BNP Paribas Asset Management will leverage its global investment platform to address systemic sustainability risks and strengthen portfolio resilience.
- Six strategic priorities: The 2026–2030 roadmap expands ESG integration, climate investment, stewardship, exclusion standards and sustainability governance.
- Regulatory and investment focus: Updated ESG methodologies, SFDR 2.0 preparations and revised net-zero targets will shape investment decisions through 2030.
BNP Paribas Asset Management (BNPP AM) has launched its Global Sustainability Strategy 2026–2030, setting out a six-pillar roadmap to strengthen investment resilience and long-term value creation.
The strategy covers more than $1.97 trillion in assets under management. As Europe’s third-largest asset manager, BNPP AM operates across listed and alternative investments, with professionals in 35 countries.
The framework responds to four megatrends reshaping global capital markets: Environment, Innovation, Demographics and Geopolitics.
BNPP AM intends to integrate these forces more deeply into investment research, portfolio construction and corporate engagement. The objective is to identify systemic risks while directing capital toward emerging opportunities in the real economy.
Six Priorities to Strengthen Sustainable Investment
The strategy establishes six priorities spanning investment research, client solutions, ESG integration, stewardship, exclusion standards and organisational accountability.
Forward-looking thematic research will strengthen analysis of climate risks, biodiversity and the Just Transition. BNPP AM also plans to finalise an updated net-zero approach ahead of revised Net Zero Asset Managers initiative (NZAM) targets in late 2026.
Client-focused solutions will address evolving sustainability regulations, including the proposed SFDR 2.0 framework. The firm will develop customised investment strategies targeting decarbonisation, environmental protection and climate resilience.
Its alternatives platform will support investments in sustainable forestry, natural capital, biodiversity and carbon solutions. These areas offer institutional investors opportunities to address environmental challenges through private-market allocations.
ESG integration will combine qualitative research with quantitative analysis to identify risks beyond traditional financial metrics.
Updated ESG and net-zero methodologies are scheduled for early 2027. BNPP AM will also expand proprietary analytical tools, dashboards and artificial intelligence capabilities to support investment decisions.
Stewardship, Exclusions and Governance
Corporate engagement will remain central to BNPP AM’s sustainability approach.
The firm plans to strengthen coordination between investment and stewardship teams across asset classes. Voting policies and issuer engagement will address climate mitigation, adaptation and emerging systemic risks.
Priority areas include responsible artificial intelligence and hazardous chemicals, alongside established environmental and governance concerns.
BNPP AM will also maintain exclusion standards designed to manage investment risks and encourage improved corporate sustainability practices.
The final pillar focuses on execution and accountability.
Stronger governance structures, transparent implementation roadmaps and enhanced fund-level reporting will support the strategy’s delivery.
Internal commitments will address operational net-zero objectives and human rights. Sustainability education, employee volunteering and philanthropic partnerships will also form part of implementation.
RELATED ARTICLE: BNP Paribas Asset Management Halts Investments in New Oil and Gas Bonds
Sustainability as a Driver of Portfolio Resilience
Jane Ambachtsheer, Chief Sustainability Officer at BNPP AM, said:
“Sustainability is a key enabler of our strategy and investment philosophy. It helps us understand risk, identify opportunity and build resilient portfolios for clients over the long term. Looking to 2030, we will deepen our insight into systemic risks, strengthen stewardship and expand our capabilities across listed and alternative assets. Just as importantly, we will embed sustainability in our culture and day-to-day decisions, matching action with ambition and supporting the communities in which we operate through volunteering and partnerships.”
The strategy places sustainability within broader investment risk management rather than treating it as a standalone consideration.
For institutional investors, the planned methodological updates could influence portfolio assessments, issuer engagement and the development of sustainability-focused products.
The emphasis on alternative assets also reflects growing interest in financing environmental outcomes beyond public equity and bond markets.
Implications for Global Sustainable Finance
BNPP AM’s roadmap arrives as European asset managers navigate evolving disclosure requirements, climate commitments and investor expectations.
SFDR reforms and updated net-zero methodologies will require firms to demonstrate how sustainability considerations translate into investment decisions and measurable outcomes.
For corporate issuers, stronger stewardship could increase scrutiny of transition strategies, environmental exposures and governance practices.
The strategy’s effectiveness will depend on implementation, particularly the consistency of ESG methodologies, engagement outcomes and fund-level disclosures.
With substantial capital deployed across global markets, BNPP AM’s approach could influence how institutional investors assess sustainability-related financial risks through 2030.
Its implementation will also provide a test of how large asset managers balance regulatory change, commercial performance and long-term climate objectives.

articles.full_text:
EU Pushes COP31 Climate Deal to Accelerate Global Emissions Cuts
- EU seeks stronger climate action: Brussels will push for a COP31 mitigation package that converts existing national climate pledges into measurable emissions reductions.
- Long-term policy oversight: The EU wants to extend the UN’s mitigation work programme until 2040, maintaining international scrutiny of emissions reduction efforts.
- Climate finance tensions: The bloc has ruled out new funding commitments at COP31, potentially deepening divisions with developing economies seeking financial support.
The European Union is preparing to push for a new global emissions reduction agreement at COP31 in Turkey this November. The initiative aims to accelerate climate action without reopening contentious negotiations over national commitments.
An internal EU document seen by Reuters outlines plans for a “mitigation package” focused on implementing existing climate pledges. The proposal reflects growing frustration over the gap between government commitments and actual emissions reductions.
The strategy comes amid mounting geopolitical tensions, worsening climate impacts and disagreements over the financial costs of decarbonisation.
EU Seeks to Extend Global Emissions Negotiations Until 2040
A central element of the EU’s COP31 strategy involves extending the United Nations’ mitigation work programme until 2040.
The programme provides a forum for governments to identify opportunities to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and strengthen climate action. It is currently scheduled to expire in 2026.
Extending the framework would preserve a dedicated international process for discussing emissions reductions over the next 14 years.
The proposal also seeks a coordinated response to the UN’s confirmation that the world will miss the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming target.
For European policymakers, maintaining international engagement on mitigation remains essential as countries face mounting pressure to deliver on existing commitments.
The draft document was prepared by Ireland, which currently holds the EU’s rotating presidency.
“We will look to strengthen our partnerships to deliver practical progress on global climate action, specifically on the transition away from fossil fuels and on electrification,” Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien said.
EU climate ministers are scheduled to discuss the bloc’s COP31 negotiating strategy on Monday.
Brussels Shifts Strategy After COP30 Negotiations Stall
The proposed approach follows disappointing outcomes at COP30 in Brazil, where governments failed to secure stronger commitments to curb greenhouse gas emissions.
Negotiations have become increasingly difficult as major emerging economies and fossil fuel-producing nations weigh climate obligations against economic development priorities.
The United States’ withdrawal from global climate negotiations has added further uncertainty to international cooperation.
Against this backdrop, EU diplomats are seeking a less confrontational approach.
Rather than pursuing public disputes over contentious negotiating positions, Brussels intends to prioritise partnerships that help countries implement existing commitments.
This includes advancing electrification and supporting the transition away from fossil fuels.
The approach places greater emphasis on delivery, potentially creating opportunities for cooperation on clean energy deployment, infrastructure investment and industrial decarbonisation.
However, its effectiveness will depend on whether governments can translate diplomatic agreements into domestic policies and measurable emissions reductions.
Climate Finance Remains a Major Obstacle
Despite its ambitions for stronger mitigation, the EU is not preparing to offer additional climate finance commitments at COP31.
The internal document states there is “no scope” for new funding pledges.
That position could complicate negotiations with developing economies, which continue to seek greater financial support for emissions reductions and climate adaptation.
Climate finance remains one of the most politically sensitive issues in international negotiations.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Backs Greenland Strategy With $232 Million
Many developing countries argue that ambitious decarbonisation targets require substantial investment in renewable energy, electricity infrastructure and cleaner industrial technologies.
Without additional financial commitments, securing broader agreement on stronger mitigation measures could prove difficult.
The EU’s position also exposes a fundamental challenge facing global climate diplomacy: aligning emissions reduction expectations with the financial capacity of individual economies.
What COP31 Means for Business and Investors
For multinational companies and institutional investors, the proposed mitigation package could influence the direction of climate policy beyond 2026.
Extending the UN mitigation work programme until 2040 would maintain international attention on national emissions trajectories and implementation progress.
That could increase pressure on governments to strengthen domestic decarbonisation policies, potentially affecting energy investment, industrial planning and corporate transition strategies.
The EU’s emphasis on electrification and fossil fuel transition also places clean energy infrastructure at the centre of its negotiating priorities.
Yet uncertainty over international climate finance could constrain investment opportunities in emerging markets, particularly where projects depend on concessional funding or public financial support.
COP31 will therefore test whether governments can advance global emissions reductions through implementation-focused cooperation, even without new financial pledges.
For the EU, the challenge extends beyond securing diplomatic consensus. Its proposed framework must deliver credible climate action while navigating competing economic priorities and increasingly fragmented international cooperation.

articles.full_text:
TotalEnergies, KKR to Expand US Solar Portfolio to 2.1 GW in $1.2B Deal
- $1.2 billion portfolio expansion: TotalEnergies and KKR plan to add 700 MW of utility-scale solar capacity across Texas and Ohio.
- 50% capacity increase: The transaction would expand their jointly owned US solar portfolio from 1.4 GW to approximately 2.1 GW.
- 2027 commercial operations: Three solar projects are expected to begin generating electricity by the first quarter of 2027, with output contracted or marketed by TotalEnergies.
TotalEnergies and global investment firm KKR plan to expand their US solar joint venture through a $1.2 billion portfolio transaction. The agreement would add 700 megawatts (MW) of renewable electricity capacity across three utility-scale projects in Texas and Ohio.
The proposed expansion would increase the partnership’s combined solar portfolio to approximately 2.1 gigawatts (GW). That represents a 50% increase from its existing 1.4 GW capacity.
The companies expect to complete the transaction during 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. All three facilities are scheduled to begin commercial operations by the first quarter of 2027.
The investment expands the companies’ exposure to US renewable electricity infrastructure as developers navigate evolving federal energy policies, financing conditions, and growing demand for power.
$1.2 Billion Transaction Expands Existing Partnership
The transaction builds on an established 50-50 joint venture between TotalEnergies and KKR. Their partnership combines institutional infrastructure investment with the French energy group’s operational expertise in electricity generation.
Under the proposed arrangement, TotalEnergies will continue operating the three solar facilities following completion.
The portfolio carries an enterprise value of $1.2 billion, although the companies have not disclosed individual project valuations or financing arrangements.
They also have not specified how the 700 MW capacity will be distributed across the Texas and Ohio facilities.
The expansion would increase the joint venture’s scale while maintaining its existing ownership structure.
For KKR, the investment adds exposure to US renewable power generation through an established operating partnership. For TotalEnergies, it expands the company’s electricity portfolio without requiring sole ownership of the underlying assets.
The arrangement illustrates how energy companies and institutional investors can share capital requirements while maintaining operational continuity across infrastructure portfolios.
Electricity Sales Provide Commercial Foundation
Electricity generated by the three facilities has either been contracted for sale to third-party customers or will be marketed directly by TotalEnergies.
This commercial structure gives the partnership multiple routes to market.
Contracted electricity sales can provide greater revenue visibility, depending on agreement terms and counterparties. Direct marketing offers flexibility but can introduce exposure to wholesale electricity prices.
The companies have not disclosed the proportion of generation covered by existing contracts, their duration, or the identity of electricity buyers.
Those details will influence how investors assess revenue stability and the portfolio’s exposure to electricity market volatility.
The location of the projects also carries commercial significance.
Texas operates one of the largest competitive electricity markets in the United States. Ohio participates in the PJM electricity market, which serves several eastern and midwestern states.
Both markets face changing electricity demand patterns, grid constraints, and questions surrounding future generation capacity.
The addition of utility-scale solar facilities will contribute new generation resources, although their economic performance will depend partly on regional market conditions and grid access.

Renewable Infrastructure Investment Faces Policy and Market Risks
The proposed transaction comes as renewable energy investors assess the implications of changing US energy policy and electricity market fundamentals.
Federal tax incentives, permitting requirements, trade measures, and equipment costs can materially affect project economics.
For utility-scale solar developers, construction schedules and grid interconnection arrangements also remain important considerations.
The companies have not disclosed whether the three facilities qualify for specific federal incentives or how potential regulatory changes could affect their financial returns.
Their planned commercial operation dates in early 2027 place project execution and timely completion among the immediate priorities.
For institutional investors, the transaction highlights the importance of evaluating renewable infrastructure beyond installed capacity alone.
Revenue contracting, operational performance, financing costs, and regulatory exposure will determine the portfolio’s long-term investment characteristics.
Strategic Implications for US Energy Investment
The planned expansion would bring TotalEnergies and KKR’s joint solar capacity to approximately 2.1 GW, strengthening their position in the US renewable electricity market.
The transaction also demonstrates continued institutional interest in utility-scale solar assets despite uncertainty surrounding the broader US energy policy environment.
For corporate electricity buyers, additional generation capacity could support renewable power procurement opportunities as facilities enter operation.
For investors, the partnership offers an example of capital deployment through shared ownership and established operational management.
Its completion will depend on the remaining transaction conditions, while the projects’ commercial performance will become clearer after operations begin in 2027.
The broader significance extends beyond the three facilities. As electricity demand and infrastructure investment requirements evolve, partnerships between energy operators and financial investors will remain an important financing model for US power generation.

Ørsted Moves to Regain Full Ownership of UK Offshore Wind Asset
Danish renewable energy developer Ørsted has exercised its right to repurchase the remaining 49.9% stake in Britain’s Gunfleet Sands offshore wind farm for $20 million.
The transaction will return full ownership of the 172-megawatt Gunfleet Sands 1 & 2 project to Ørsted. It also gives the company greater control over decisions concerning the ageing asset’s operational future.
Located approximately seven kilometres off England’s southeastern coast, Gunfleet Sands has generated renewable electricity since 2010.
Before the transaction, Ørsted held a controlling 50.1% interest in the project. Japanese power generator JERA and the Development Bank of Japan (DBJ) each owned 24.95%.
The acquisition follows a longstanding repurchase right established under the original partnership agreement. Completion is expected in November.
The move comes as Europe’s offshore wind industry faces growing questions about asset longevity, operating costs and investment priorities.
Lifetime Extension Becomes a Strategic Priority
Ørsted said the acquisition will allow it to evaluate future options for Gunfleet Sands, including a potential extension of the wind farm’s operational lifetime.
The project has operated for approximately 16 years, placing it among Britain’s earlier commercial offshore wind developments.
Its 172 MW capacity generates enough renewable electricity to supply more than 125,000 UK homes annually.
For offshore wind operators, extending the useful life of existing installations offers an alternative to developing replacement generation capacity.
Such decisions require detailed assessments of turbine condition, maintenance requirements, structural integrity and future electricity production.
Operators must also consider whether additional capital expenditure can deliver sufficient returns over an extended operating period.
For Gunfleet Sands, Ørsted’s renewed ownership provides a clearer framework for evaluating these options without coordinating decisions across multiple shareholders.
However, the company has not announced a final decision on extending the project’s lifetime.
Japanese Investors Exit Established Renewable Energy Partnership
The transaction will end JERA’s and DBJ’s ownership interests in Gunfleet Sands, consolidating the project under Ørsted.
Both Japanese investors previously held equal minority stakes, reflecting the international capital partnerships that have supported offshore wind development.
Such arrangements allow developers to share financial exposure while providing institutional investors access to established renewable energy infrastructure.
The original agreement also included a mechanism enabling Ørsted to repurchase those interests.
By exercising that contractual right, Ørsted can reassess the asset’s future under a single ownership structure.
The $20 million purchase price covers the combined 49.9% stake. It does not represent the total historical investment in the project or the cost of extending its operating life.
The transaction also illustrates how ownership structures can evolve as renewable energy assets move from development into mature operational phases.

UK Offshore Wind Sector Faces Long-Term Asset Decisions
Britain remains one of Europe’s largest offshore wind markets, with the technology central to its electricity decarbonisation strategy.
Maintaining generation from existing installations will become increasingly important as early offshore projects approach their original design lifetimes.
For developers, the financial calculation extends beyond electricity output.
Older turbines may require additional maintenance, replacement components and engineering assessments. These costs must be weighed against projected revenues and the expense of developing new capacity.
Lifetime extensions could preserve renewable generation while delaying some decommissioning expenditure. However, their commercial viability depends on asset-specific technical and financial conditions.
For investors, these decisions introduce new considerations around infrastructure valuation, operational risk and capital allocation.
Implications for Renewable Energy Investors
Ørsted’s acquisition gives the company full control over Gunfleet Sands as it considers the project’s next operational phase.
The immediate financial commitment is relatively modest compared with the capital required to develop new offshore wind installations.
Nevertheless, any subsequent lifetime extension would require a separate investment assessment.
For the wider renewable energy industry, Gunfleet Sands reflects an increasingly important challenge: determining how to maximise the economic and environmental value of existing infrastructure.
As Europe’s first generations of offshore wind farms mature, ownership consolidation, lifetime extensions and eventual decommissioning will become central to investment decisions.
Ørsted’s next steps at Gunfleet Sands could offer insight into how established offshore wind assets fit within Britain’s longer-term clean energy ambitions.

IFC and BlueOrchard Target $2 Billion in Emerging Market Investment The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and BlueOrchard Finance have partnered to mobilize up to $2 billion in institutional capital for […]
The post IFC, BlueOrchard Launch $2 Billion Emerging Markets Private Debt Fund appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
IFC, BlueOrchard Launch $2 Billion Emerging Markets Private Debt Fund
- $2 billion investment target: IFC and BlueOrchard have launched an evergreen private debt vehicle to mobilize institutional capital for emerging markets.
- $300 million secured: Tokio Marine Group anchors the first closing, supporting investment in businesses that generate employment and economic growth.
- $25.5 billion investment platform: The initiative builds on IFC’s Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program, expanding institutional access to emerging market private credit.
IFC and BlueOrchard Target $2 Billion in Emerging Market Investment
The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and BlueOrchard Finance have partnered to mobilize up to $2 billion in institutional capital for emerging market private debt investments.
The initiative, backed by the World Bank Group’s private sector investment arm, aims to address persistent financing gaps in developing economies. It will channel long-term capital toward businesses that support employment, economic development, and financial inclusion.
Tokio Marine Group has joined as the anchor investor, contributing to a $300 million first closing.
The partnership combines IFC’s investment origination capabilities with BlueOrchard’s experience managing emerging market debt portfolios. BlueOrchard, a member of Schroders Group, brings 25 years of investment experience across developing economies.
The structure seeks to attract pension funds, insurance companies, and sovereign wealth funds seeking diversified private credit exposure.
“Emerging markets need trillions of dollars to invest in their development—far more than public finance can supply,” said Makhtar Diop, IFC Managing Director. “This initiative with BlueOrchard and Tokio Marine Group creates a scalable way to connect institutional capital with businesses that create jobs, expand opportunities and improve lives in the places that need it the most.”
Evergreen Structure Expands Institutional Access to Private Credit
Unlike traditional closed-end investment funds, the new vehicle operates through an evergreen structure.
Investors can subscribe and redeem capital on an ongoing basis, subject to predefined redemption windows. Investment proceeds can also be reinvested into new opportunities, allowing capital to circulate across successive lending transactions.
This approach provides institutional investors with a long-term allocation mechanism while supporting continued financing for emerging market borrowers.
The structure also addresses a longstanding challenge for institutional investors: accessing diversified private credit portfolios in markets where direct investment can involve significant operational and regulatory complexity.
“Institutional investors are increasingly looking for long-term private credit opportunities that combine returns and diversification with access to emerging markets,” said Michael Wehrle, CEO of BlueOrchard. “With 25 years of experience investing across these markets and building diversified and resilient portfolios, we can provide that access at scale while directing capital to where it can have meaningful impact.”

Tokio Marine Anchors $300 Million First Closing
Tokio Marine Group’s participation extends its longstanding investment relationship with IFC.
The Japanese insurance group has supported IFC’s efforts to mobilize private capital across emerging markets for several years. Its anchor commitment provides an institutional foundation for the vehicle’s expansion toward its $2 billion target.
“This investment marks a natural next step in Tokio Marine Group’s longstanding partnership with IFC. Combining IFC’s origination capabilities with BlueOrchard’s 25-year track record in managing diversified emerging market debt portfolios gives us access, at scale, to a segment of private credit that has traditionally been difficult for institutional investors to reach. We are pleased to deepen our collaboration with IFC and BlueOrchard through this investment. We are proud to bring our long-term institutional capital to this initiative, which will help support sustainable and resilient economic growth and create jobs in emerging markets,” said Masahiro Koike, Group CEO, Tokio Marine Holdings, Inc.
Building on IFC’s $25.5 Billion Co-Lending Platform
The investment vehicle expands IFC’s Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program (MCPP), established in 2013.
MCPP currently has more than $25.5 billion in investment capacity. The platform enables institutional partners to co-invest alongside IFC in emerging market loans on commercial terms.
The new structure adapts this model for a broader institutional investor base, potentially increasing the availability of long-term private financing.
IFC and BlueOrchard are entering the market following two decades of improvements in emerging market debt fundamentals. Stronger regulatory frameworks, improved governance, and declining default rates have helped support investor confidence.
For institutional allocators, the initiative offers access to markets where credit diversification and development outcomes can intersect.
Its broader significance lies in mobilizing private investment beyond traditional development finance channels. As emerging economies confront substantial infrastructure, employment, and sustainable development financing needs, scalable private credit structures could help narrow funding gaps without relying exclusively on public capital.

articles.summary:

articles.full_text:
Adidas, H&M and Inditex Launch Coalition to Tackle Global Textile Waste
- Industry collaboration: Adidas, H&M Group, Inditex and Bestseller have launched the Apparel Recovery Coalition to address global textile waste and strengthen circular fashion systems.
- Two-year initiative: The coalition will test producer responsibility models, fund textile recovery projects and improve waste management in countries receiving secondhand clothing exports.
- Environmental accountability: Ghana’s Kantamanto Market processes approximately 25 million garments monthly, highlighting the environmental and social costs of global textile consumption.
Fashion Giants Join Forces to Address Textile Waste
Accra, Ghana has become the launchpad for a new industry initiative aimed at addressing the environmental consequences of global textile waste.
Adidas, H&M Group, Zara-owner Inditex and Danish fashion company Bestseller have established the Apparel Recovery Coalition (ARC). The initiative brings major fashion producers together with Ghana-based nonprofit The Or Foundation and circular economy organization Circle Economy.
The coalition will examine how fashion brands can assume greater responsibility for clothing after consumers discard it. Its focus includes reuse, recycling, upcycling and improved waste management in countries receiving large volumes of secondhand textiles.
The two-year initiative will develop and test a producer responsibility business model that reflects international textile trade flows.
It also aims to bring brands, recyclers, sorting companies, policymakers and affected communities into discussions about practical waste management solutions.
The initiative arrives as fashion companies face increasing pressure to address the environmental consequences of production, consumption and textile exports.
Ghana’s Kantamanto Market Becomes Testing Ground
The coalition launched at Kantamanto Market in Accra, one of the world’s largest centers for secondhand clothing trade and textile recovery.
According to The Or Foundation, the market recirculates approximately 25 million garments every month.
Thousands of traders, repairers and other workers contribute to an extensive informal circular economy. Their activities extend the useful life of clothing that might otherwise enter waste streams.
However, the market also illustrates the environmental challenges associated with international secondhand textile exports.
Clothing that cannot be resold or recovered can contribute to waste accumulation, water contamination and soil pollution. Local communities and waste management systems bear much of the resulting burden.
ARC intends to build on The Or Foundation’s 15 years of work supporting Ghana’s circular textile ecosystem.
The coalition states that it will “test more inclusive approaches to governance, design, and implementation” by incorporating community perspectives into its activities.
Its first demonstration project will operate in Accra, supporting infrastructure improvements, environmental remediation and training initiatives.
A second demonstration project is planned for another country receiving substantial volumes of secondhand clothing.
Fashion Brands Commit Funding to Circular Recovery
Adidas, H&M Group, Inditex and Bestseller will provide voluntary financial contributions to support the coalition’s demonstration projects.
The companies have not disclosed the total funding commitment.
The initiative will examine how extended producer responsibility frameworks could support textile recovery across international supply chains.
Such frameworks require producers to assume greater financial or operational responsibility for products after their useful life ends.
For fashion companies, this could eventually influence product design, waste management costs and investment in recycling infrastructure.
The coalition expects its findings to inform future industry practices and regulatory approaches.
“The coalition hopes the evidence and practical learnings generated through these demonstration projects will help inform brands, policymakers, producer responsibility organizations (PROs) and other stakeholders working to strengthen post-consumer textile management systems worldwide,” the release said.
RELATED ARTICLE: Textile Waste: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
Rising Production Volumes Intensify Environmental Scrutiny
The initiative comes amid growing scrutiny of the fashion industry’s resource consumption and waste generation.
Inditex reported using 705,554 metric tons of raw materials in its products, compared with 678,596 metric tons in 2024.
That represents an increase of approximately 4%, illustrating the scale of material demand across its operations.
Meanwhile, H&M Group reported producing 364,093 metric tons of products in 2025, equivalent to approximately 36 Eiffel Towers.
These figures highlight the challenge facing fashion companies attempting to reconcile commercial growth with circular economy commitments.
Recovery and recycling initiatives can reduce waste impacts, but their effectiveness also depends on product durability, material choices and production volumes.
For investors, the coalition introduces another area for evaluating corporate sustainability performance: whether voluntary industry commitments produce measurable improvements in textile recovery and environmental management.
Producer Responsibility Could Reshape Global Textile Governance
The coalition plans to expand participation among additional companies and stakeholders as its work progresses.
Its findings could help policymakers assess how producer responsibility systems should account for textiles exported across national borders.
This remains a significant governance challenge. Products often reach the end of their useful lives far from the countries where brands originally sold them.
For multinational fashion companies, stronger accountability could create additional compliance obligations and financing requirements.
For importing countries, effective producer responsibility mechanisms could provide resources for infrastructure, environmental protection and local circular businesses.
The coalition’s longer-term relevance will depend on whether its demonstration projects deliver practical, scalable financing and recovery models.
As governments and investors increase scrutiny of fashion’s environmental footprint, Ghana’s textile recovery economy could help shape how global brands manage responsibility beyond the point of sale.
